chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr and Muhammad ibn Isa, all from Yunus, from Umar ibn Udhaynah, who said:

I said to Zurarah: 'Indeed, some people narrated to me from him, meaning Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), and from his father (peace be upon him), about various matters in inheritance. So I will present them to you. Whatever of them is false, say
He said: 'By Allah, this is false. But I will inform you and not narrate to you anything (as a formal hadith), and what I tell you is, by Allah, the truth.'

When a man leaves his parents, the mother gets one-third and the father gets two-thirds in the Book of Allah. If he has brothers, meaning for the deceased, brothers from father and mother or brothers from father, then for his mother is one-sixth and for the father five-sixths. And the father's share was increased on account of his dependents.
As for brothers from the mother who are not from the father, they do not block the mother from the one-third, nor do they inherit.

And if a man dies and leaves his mother, and brothers and sisters from father and mother, and brothers and sisters from father, and brothers and sisters from mother, and the father is not alive, then they do not inherit and do not block her, because he did not inherit as a Kalalah (one with no parents or children).

key_terms.كَلَالَةً: Deceased with no direct descendants or ascendants

ai.seo_question: What are the inheritance shares of parents and siblings according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Zurarah clarifies the nuanced inheritance rules for parents and siblings, distinguishing between full, paternal, and maternal siblings. He explains that while the mother's share is reduced by the presence of any siblings, the father's share increases to five-sixths specifically to support his dependents, whereas maternal siblings do not block the mother's share nor inherit themselves due to the absence of a 'Kalala' (parental) link. This narration highlights the Shia jurisprudential emphasis on the father's role as a provider and the specific conditions under which siblings are excluded from inheritance.
